moments.title: The Mandelbrot set
moments.body:
Mandelbrot, using IBM's computers, plots the set of complex numbers c such that iterating z to z^2 + c (starting from z = 0) stays bounded.

The resulting image — a black cardioid-and-circle shape with an infinitely complex boundary — has become one of the most iconic images in mathematics. The boundary has Hausdorff dimension 2.

Brooks and Matelski had plotted similar things in 1978 but Mandelbrot's images, and his book 'The Fractal Geometry of Nature' (1982), popularise fractals globally.
moments.takeaway: The Mandelbrot set is computed and visualised. The fractal aesthetic spreads beyond mathematics.

moments.title: Fractals enter culture and applications
moments.body:
Fractals appear in:
- Computer graphics (mountain landscape generation in films).
- Physics (turbulence, fluid dynamics, polymer physics).
- Biology (lung branching, vascular networks, fern growth).
- Finance (Mandelbrot's later work on financial market fractality).
- Art (Mandelbrot set zooms; pattern design).

Fractal antennas (transmitting/receiving across many frequencies) are commercially important. Compression algorithms (fractal image compression) compete with JPEG.
moments.takeaway: Fractals become an interdisciplinary toolkit and cultural phenomenon.

now.title: Fractals today
now.body:
Fractal geometry is a standard part of nonlinear dynamics, complexity science, and computer graphics. Self-similar structures appear in scale-free networks (social, biological), chaotic attractors, and many natural systems.

Applications: rough surface modelling, fluid simulation, biological tissue modelling, image compression, antenna design.
now.open_questions: Why is so much of nature fractal? Are there 'higher-order' fractal-like structures we haven't recognised? Can fractal dimensions be efficiently computed for real-world data? Are there fractal analogs in higher mathematics?

items.reflection: Mandelbrot worked at IBM rather than in academia partly because he was an outsider — a Polish Jewish immigrant whose mathematical instincts were geometric and applied in an era of abstract Bourbaki-style mathematics. His insights were rejected for years. How often does breakthrough understanding come from people working outside the institutions that should reward them?

moments.title: Fermat's marginal note
moments.body:
Fermat writes in the margin of his copy of Diophantus's Arithmetica: 'It is impossible to separate a cube into two cubes, or a fourth power into two fourth powers, or in general, any power higher than the second, into two like powers. I have discovered a truly marvellous proof of this, which this margin is too narrow to contain.'

Fermat dies in 1665. His son Samuel finds the marginal notes and publishes them in 1670. The 'truly marvellous proof' is never found.
moments.takeaway: A 358-year mathematical puzzle is launched by a margin note.

moments.title: Centuries of partial progress
moments.body:
Euler (1770) proves the case n = 3. Sophie Germain (early 1800s) makes important progress (the 'Sophie Germain theorem' handles many cases). Dirichlet (1828) and Legendre (1830) prove case n = 5. Lamé (1839) handles n = 7.

Kummer (1840s) introduces ideal numbers (later called ideals), settling many more cases. His framework becomes essential for modern algebraic number theory.
moments.takeaway: Fermat's challenge drives major developments in number theory for centuries.

moments.title: Taniyama-Shimura and Frey-Ribet
moments.who: Yutaka Taniyama, Goro Shimura, André Weil, Gerhard Frey, Ken Ribet
moments.body:
Yutaka Taniyama (1955) conjectures a deep connection between elliptic curves and modular forms (he commits suicide in 1958). Shimura and Weil refine the conjecture: all elliptic curves over the rationals are modular.

Gerhard Frey (1985) shows that a non-trivial Fermat solution would give a non-modular elliptic curve (the Frey curve). Ken Ribet (1986) proves that no such curve can be modular. If Taniyama-Shimura is true, Fermat follows.
moments.takeaway: Fermat's Last Theorem reduces to a deep central conjecture of modern number theory.

moments.title: Wiles works in secret
moments.body:
Andrew Wiles, who had been fascinated by Fermat since reading about it at age 10, decides to attack Taniyama-Shimura for the class of curves Fermat needed. He works in his attic for 7 years in near-total secrecy.

Only his wife knows. He stops attending most conferences. He publishes nothing during this period to avoid hinting at his progress.

In May 1993, he completes a proof. He plans his announcement carefully.
moments.takeaway: One of the longest secret research projects in mathematical history.

moments.title: Announcement, gap, and completion
moments.body:
23 June 1993: Wiles announces the proof at the Isaac Newton Institute in Cambridge. The audience erupts. Newspapers cover the proof of 'the most famous unsolved problem in mathematics'.

A referee finds a gap in the proof in autumn 1993. The proof relied on a step that wasn't quite right. Wiles works for a year, with help from his former student Richard Taylor, to repair it.

In September 1994, Wiles finds the missing piece in a moment of insight. The repaired proof is submitted in October 1994 and published as two papers in Annals of Mathematics in 1995.

quote.attrib: Andrew Wiles, at the end of his 1993 Cambridge lecture

moments.takeaway: Seven years of secret work, then a year of public crisis, then triumph. Fermat's Last Theorem is proved.

now.title: Modular forms and elliptic curves today
now.body:
Wiles's proof of Fermat's Last Theorem also proved most of the Taniyama-Shimura conjecture for elliptic curves over the rationals. The full conjecture (modularity theorem) was completed by Breuil, Conrad, Diamond and Taylor in 2001.

The techniques have been extended: Sato-Tate conjecture (proved by Clozel, Harris, Shepherd-Barron, Taylor 2008-2011). The Langlands program — Robert Langlands's vast web of conjectures connecting number theory, automorphic forms, and Galois representations — is the central guiding vision of modern number theory.
now.open_questions: Can the Langlands program be completed? What other classical-sounding problems can be reduced to modularity-style statements? Did Fermat have any kind of proof at all? (Almost certainly not — he never repeated the claim and his methods could only have handled n = 4, which he did separately publish.)

items.reflection: Fermat almost certainly didn't have a proof. His margin note was probably wishful thinking. Yet that mistake drove 358 years of mathematics, including some of the deepest developments of the field. How much of mathematical progress is driven by problems that turn out to be ill-posed or based on errors? Is Goldbach's conjecture another such case waiting to be cracked?

moments.title: Brahmagupta defines arithmetic with zero
moments.body:
Brahmagupta writes 'Brahmasphutasiddhanta', containing the first systematic treatment of zero as a number (not just a placeholder). He gives rules: a + 0 = a, a - 0 = a, a x 0 = 0. He also gives rules for negative numbers ('debts' as opposed to 'fortunes').

He is the first to write rules for arithmetic with positive, negative, and zero quantities — including the (incorrect, as he wrote it) rule for division by zero.
moments.takeaway: Zero and negative numbers enter mathematics as legitimate quantities, with consistent arithmetic rules.

moments.title: Al-Khwarizmi transmits to the Arab world
moments.body:
Al-Khwarizmi, working at the House of Wisdom in Baghdad, writes treatises on arithmetic (using Hindu numerals) and 'al-jabr' (algebra). The Hindu-Arabic numeral system, including zero, becomes standard in Arab mathematics.

The word 'algorithm' derives from al-Khwarizmi's name (latinised: Algoritmi). The word 'algebra' from his treatise's title 'Al-Kitāb al-mukhtaṣar fī ḥisāb al-jabr wa-l-muqābala'.
moments.takeaway: Indian mathematics travels to the Islamic world. The numeral system that will eventually dominate Europe takes shape.

moments.title: Fibonacci brings the system to Europe
moments.body:
Fibonacci, having travelled in North Africa and learned arithmetic with Hindu-Arabic numerals, writes 'Liber Abaci' (1202). He promotes the system as far superior to Roman numerals for calculation.

Merchants begin adopting it for accounting. The transition is slow — Roman numerals dominate official documents in Europe for another 300+ years.
moments.takeaway: Indian-Arabic numerals reach Europe. Calculation becomes vastly more practical.

moments.title: Europe accepts negative numbers reluctantly
moments.body:
Cardano (1545) uses negative numbers as 'fictitious' quantities — useful for calculation but ontologically suspect. Descartes (1637) calls negative roots of equations 'false roots'.

European mathematicians struggle with negatives until the 1700s. Many texts continue calling them 'impossible' or 'absurd'. The full acceptance of negative numbers comes only with the formalisation of arithmetic in the 19th century.
moments.takeaway: Europe takes centuries to fully accept what Indian mathematicians had codified a millennium earlier.

moments.title: Peano axioms
moments.body:
Giuseppe Peano publishes the Peano axioms, a rigorous formal foundation for the natural numbers based on five postulates. Zero (or one) is the starting point; succession defines the rest.

Later work (Frege, Russell, Whitehead, Dedekind) extends this to integers (positive and negative), rationals, reals, and complex numbers. Each extension is constructed from the previous.
moments.takeaway: The natural numbers — including zero — are given a rigorous axiomatic foundation. Modern number systems are formally constructed.

now.title: Number systems today
now.body:
Numbers come in many varieties: natural (0, 1, 2, ...), integers (negatives included), rationals (fractions), reals (limits of rationals), complex (with i), quaternions (4D), octonions (8D), p-adic numbers, surreal numbers (Conway, infinitely many infinities and infinitesimals).

In computing: integers are typically stored in fixed-width binary (signed and unsigned); reals are approximated with floating-point (IEEE 754 standards).
now.open_questions: Are there number systems we haven't discovered that would simplify some current mathematics? Why are some constants (pi, e) so deeply connected that e^(i*pi) + 1 = 0? Can the 'mathematical reality' of larger number systems (e.g., complex numbers in quantum mechanics) be derived rather than postulated?

items.reflection: Zero was invented in India and traveled through the Arab world to Europe. Negative numbers were widely accepted in India by 600 AD and rejected by European mathematicians as 'absurd' as late as the 18th century. The mathematical tools we now consider elementary took millennia to develop and to spread. How does mathematical culture transmit, and why does it sometimes take centuries to accept what other cultures have already mastered?

moments.title: Babylonian and Egyptian approximations
moments.body:
Babylonian tablet (~1900 BC): pi ≈ 3.125. Egyptian Rhind Papyrus (~1650 BC): pi ≈ (16/9)^2 = 3.16049... Both within ~1% of the true value.

These are practical engineering approximations, not theoretical results. The ratio of circumference to diameter is known to be roughly 3 by every civilisation that built round structures.
moments.takeaway: Pi was known approximately by every ancient civilisation. None had a method to compute it precisely.

moments.title: Archimedes inscribes and circumscribes polygons
moments.body:
Archimedes uses 96-sided polygons inscribed in and circumscribed around a circle to bound pi: 223/71 < pi < 22/7. That is, 3.1408... < pi < 3.1428...

This 'method of exhaustion' is the first rigorous method for computing pi. It anticipates calculus by 2000 years.
moments.takeaway: Archimedes gives the first systematic method for computing pi to any desired precision.

moments.title: Viète's product formula
moments.body:
François Viète gives the first INFINITE expression for pi: an infinite product involving nested square roots of 2. The first analytical formula for pi as a limit.

Various infinite series and products follow: Wallis (1655), Leibniz (1674: 1 - 1/3 + 1/5 - 1/7 + ... = pi/4), Machin (1706: pi/4 = 4 arctan(1/5) - arctan(1/239), accelerating convergence).
moments.takeaway: Pi becomes computable in principle to any precision via infinite series.

moments.title: Lambert proves pi irrational
moments.body:
Lambert proves that pi is irrational — it cannot be written as a ratio of integers. The proof uses continued fractions.

This settles a question debated for millennia. Pi has no exact decimal expansion; its digits cannot eventually repeat.
moments.takeaway: Pi is irrational. Whatever decimal expansion you compute, it never repeats.

moments.title: Lindemann proves pi transcendental
moments.body:
Lindemann proves pi is transcendental — it is not the root of any polynomial with integer coefficients.

Consequence: the ancient problem of 'squaring the circle' (constructing a square with the same area as a given circle using only compass and straightedge) is impossible. Compass-and-straightedge constructions can only produce algebraic numbers; pi isn't algebraic.

This settles a problem posed by Greek geometers nearly 2500 years earlier.
moments.takeaway: Pi is transcendental. An ancient problem is resolved — negatively.

now.title: Pi today
now.body:
Pi has been computed to over 100 trillion digits (Google Cloud, 2022). The Chudnovsky algorithm and similar series allow rapid computation. The Bailey-Borwein-Plouffe formula (1995) lets you compute the nth hexadecimal digit of pi WITHOUT computing the previous digits — a feat once thought impossible.

Pi appears throughout mathematics (in many integrals, sums, products) and physics (Heisenberg uncertainty principle, the Einstein field equations, optics, electromagnetism).
now.open_questions: Is pi 'normal' in any base — does every digit appear with the right frequency? (Strongly suspected, never proved.) What constants are transcendental? (e, pi are; e + pi is unknown!) Why does pi appear in so many seemingly unrelated areas of mathematics?

items.reflection: Pi has been the subject of computation for 4000 years. The motivations have shifted: practical engineering (3 to 1%), theoretical curiosity (Archimedes), test of computational power (modern records). What does it mean to 'know' a number whose digits go on forever and never repeat? At what point does additional precision become meaningless — and what motivates us to compute trillions of digits?

moments.title: Al-Khwarizmi at the House of Wisdom
moments.body:
The Abbasid Caliph al-Ma'mun establishes the House of Wisdom in Baghdad as a centre of learning. Scholars translate Greek, Persian, and Indian works into Arabic and produce original research.

Al-Khwarizmi writes a treatise: 'Al-Kitāb al-mukhtaṣar fī ḥisāb al-jabr wa-l-muqābala' — 'The Compendious Book on Calculation by Completion and Balancing'.

He systematically solves linear and quadratic equations using algebraic manipulation. The word 'algebra' is from 'al-jabr' (completion/restoration — moving a negative term to the other side). 'Al-Khwarizmi' Latinised to 'Algoritmi' gives us 'algorithm'.
moments.takeaway: Algebra is born as a discipline. The methods, the name, and the word 'algorithm' all come from al-Khwarizmi.

moments.title: Hindu numerals in Arabic mathematics
moments.body:
Al-Khwarizmi also writes a treatise on Hindu arithmetic, introducing the Indian decimal place-value system (with zero) to the Arab world. The original Arabic text is lost; we know it only through Latin translations.

The numerals 0-9, plus the place-value system, become standard in Arab mathematics. This is the system that will eventually conquer the world.
moments.takeaway: Indian numerals enter the Arab tradition. The system that we now call 'Arabic numerals' is mostly Indian, transmitted via Arabic-speaking scholars.

moments.title: Robert of Chester translates al-Khwarizmi
moments.body:
Robert of Chester translates al-Khwarizmi's algebra into Latin in Toledo or nearby. The Latin Christian world begins to acquire Arabic mathematical knowledge through Spain and Sicily.

The Toledo School of Translators becomes a major channel for Arabic science to reach Europe. Aristotle's Greek works also come back to Europe via Arabic translations of Greek originals.
moments.takeaway: Arabic mathematics enters medieval Europe. The transmission is slow but transformative.

moments.title: Fibonacci's Liber Abaci
moments.body:
Fibonacci, having travelled in North Africa with his merchant father, learns Arabic arithmetic. He writes 'Liber Abaci' (Book of Calculation) to promote the new numerals and methods in Italy.

The book includes the Fibonacci sequence (1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, ...) in a problem about rabbit populations. The sequence — a small footnote in his book — becomes one of his lasting legacies.

Merchants gradually adopt the new system, though European bureaucracies stick with Roman numerals for centuries longer.
moments.takeaway: Italian merchants adopt Arabic numerals first. Banking, accounting and modern commerce become possible at scale.

moments.title: Symbolic algebra emerges
moments.body:
François Viète (1591) introduces letters for unknowns AND known quantities — symbolic algebra. Descartes (1637) standardises the conventions we still use (x, y, z for unknowns; a, b, c for constants; exponential notation).

These conventions are part of the 'algebra' we now teach in schools. Al-Khwarizmi's prose-based algebra has been largely superseded — but the methods are the same.
moments.takeaway: Algebra becomes symbolic in 17th-century Europe. The rhetorical algebra of medieval texts gives way to formulas.

now.title: Algebra today
now.body:
Algebra is the language of mathematics. Linear algebra, abstract algebra (groups, rings, fields), algebraic geometry, commutative algebra, homological algebra — all descend from al-Khwarizmi's original effort to systematise solutions to equations.

Computer algebra systems (Mathematica, Maple, SymPy, Sage) automate vast portions of algebraic manipulation. Symbolic computation is essential to physics, engineering, and many areas of mathematics.
now.open_questions: Can we automate higher-level algebra reasoning beyond what current systems do? What's the right balance between symbolic and numerical methods? Are there algebraic structures we haven't yet discovered that would simplify current problems?

items.reflection: Algebra is named after an Arabic word; algorithm is named after an Arabic name; our numerals were transmitted through Arabic mathematics. Yet many Western histories of mathematics jump from Greece to Renaissance Europe, omitting the Islamic Golden Age. What does it mean for a discipline to know its history honestly? And how should mathematical education reflect the global, multicultural origins of the field?

moments.title: Sophie Germain corresponds under a man's name
moments.body:
Sophie Germain teaches herself mathematics from her father's library during the French Revolution. Women are not admitted to the École Polytechnique. She acquires lecture notes by a male friend and submits her work under the pseudonym 'Antoine-August Le Blanc'.

Lagrange notices the quality of 'M. Le Blanc's' work and asks to meet him. Germain reveals herself. Lagrange becomes her mentor.

She corresponds with Carl Friedrich Gauss under the Le Blanc name for years. When Napoleon's army threatens Gauss in Brunswick (1806), she writes to a French general asking that Gauss be protected — revealing her real identity in the process. Gauss writes that her gender 'gives her the right to admiration and esteem'.
moments.takeaway: A self-taught woman with no institutional access produces serious mathematics, including major progress on Fermat's Last Theorem.

moments.title: Sophie Germain wins the elasticity prize
moments.body:
The French Academy of Sciences offers a prize for explaining the vibration patterns of elastic plates (Chladni patterns). Germain wins on her third attempt (1816). She is the first woman to win a prize from the Academy.

She is not allowed to attend the Academy's meetings — women are excluded.

Her work on Fermat's Last Theorem — 'Germain's theorem' handling certain prime exponents — anticipates the use of ideals in number theory by Kummer decades later.
moments.takeaway: Germain's elasticity work is foundational to modern continuum mechanics. She is excluded from the institutions that should celebrate her.

moments.title: Sofya Kovalevskaya
moments.body:
Sofya Kovalevskaya — Russian mathematician — becomes the first woman to receive a doctorate in mathematics in modern Europe (Göttingen, 1874). She is appointed professor at Stockholm University in 1889 — the first woman to hold a full professorship in modern Europe.

Her work on partial differential equations (Cauchy-Kovalevskaya theorem), rotation of solid bodies, and mathematical physics is fundamental.
moments.takeaway: The first European woman to hold a mathematics chair. The barriers crumble slowly.

moments.title: Emmy Noether at Erlangen and Göttingen
moments.body:
Emmy Noether earns her doctorate in 1907 (Erlangen). She works without pay for 7 years (women are not allowed to be paid as university teachers).

In 1915, Hilbert and Klein bring her to Göttingen. Hilbert tries to get her habilitated (the qualification to lecture) — the faculty refuses on the grounds that she's a woman.

Hilbert: 'Gentlemen, the faculty is not a bathing establishment.' She is finally granted habilitation in 1919 after the German Republic changes the laws.

Noether proves the theorem now bearing her name (1915, published 1918): every continuous symmetry corresponds to a conservation law. This is one of the deepest insights in physics — explaining why energy, momentum, charge are conserved.
moments.takeaway: Noether's theorem becomes a foundational result in physics. She had to fight for the right to teach.

moments.title: Noether expelled by Nazis, dies in America
moments.body:
The Nazi laws of 1933 expel Jewish academics from German universities. Noether is dismissed from Göttingen.

She moves to Bryn Mawr College in the United States. She becomes a leader of the abstract algebra revolution — her work on commutative rings, ideals, and group representations transforms the field. She is one of the founders of modern abstract algebra.

She dies in 1935 of complications from surgery, age 53. Einstein writes a tribute in the New York Times calling her 'the most significant creative mathematical genius thus far produced since the higher education of women began'.
moments.takeaway: Noether transforms abstract algebra. She dies young, with much undone. Mathematics rebuilds on her foundations for the next century.

now.title: Women in mathematics today
now.body:
Maryam Mirzakhani (2014) became the first woman to win the Fields Medal — almost 80 years after its founding. Karen Uhlenbeck (Abel Prize 2019), Maryna Viazovska (Fields Medal 2022). Many women now lead major mathematical projects.

But representation remains uneven: women are about 30% of math PhDs in many countries, fewer at senior levels. Bias and culture-of-exclusion issues persist.
now.open_questions: How do we close the gender gap in mathematics? How much past achievement has been suppressed or unattributed? What would mathematics look like if women had had equal access for centuries?

items.reflection: Sophie Germain wrote under a man's name. Emmy Noether worked unpaid for years. Sofya Kovalevskaya was the first European woman professor of mathematics in centuries. The mathematics they produced is foundational. How much was lost to systematic exclusion? How do we reckon with what wasn't done by the women who never got the chance to try?

moments.title: Poincaré and the three-body problem
moments.body:
King Oscar II of Sweden offers a prize for solving the three-body problem in celestial mechanics: predict the motion of three gravitating bodies. The two-body problem has elegant Keplerian solutions; the three-body problem had defeated everyone.

Poincaré wins the prize in 1889 — but the original prize-winning paper contained an error. While correcting it, he discovers that the three-body problem can have orbits that are extraordinarily sensitive to initial conditions: small changes in starting conditions produce wildly different outcomes.

He doesn't quite call it 'chaos', but he discovers its essential feature.
moments.takeaway: Even simple Newtonian gravitational systems can be unpredictable. Determinism doesn't guarantee predictability.

moments.title: Lorenz's truncated simulation
moments.body:
Lorenz, an MIT meteorologist, runs a simulation of atmospheric convection using a Royal McBee LGP-30 computer (1500 transistors, ~1 kHz clock). He restarts a calculation from intermediate data, entering numbers as printed (3 decimal places) rather than as internally stored (6 decimal places).

The new run diverges completely from the original within a simulated month. Lorenz realises the small rounding errors are growing exponentially.
moments.takeaway: Tiny errors in initial conditions grow into completely different futures. Weather simulation discovers chaos.

moments.title: 'Deterministic Nonperiodic Flow'
moments.who: Edward Lorenz, Journal of the Atmospheric Sciences
moments.body:
Lorenz publishes a paper introducing what we now call the Lorenz attractor: a system of three coupled differential equations with a beautiful, butterfly-shaped trajectory that never repeats but is bounded.

The paper is read mostly by meteorologists. It will be 10+ years before nonlinear dynamics and chaos theory catch the attention of mathematicians.
moments.takeaway: The first famous strange attractor is published. The paper is barely noticed.

moments.title: Lorenz's butterfly talk
moments.body:
Lorenz gives a talk titled 'Predictability: Does the Flap of a Butterfly's Wings in Brazil Set Off a Tornado in Texas?' The butterfly effect enters cultural vocabulary.

Meanwhile, mathematicians (Stephen Smale, David Ruelle, Floris Takens) develop nonlinear dynamics. James Yorke and Tien-Yien Li coin the term 'chaos' in mathematics (1975).

quote.text: Chaos: when the present determines the future, but the approximate present does not approximately determine the future.

moments.takeaway: The butterfly effect captures public imagination. Chaos becomes a recognised mathematical discipline.

moments.title: Chaos in popular science
moments.who: Robert May, Mitchell Feigenbaum, James Gleick
moments.body:
Robert May (1976) publishes a Nature paper showing how the logistic map produces chaotic dynamics — bringing chaos to ecology.

Mitchell Feigenbaum (1978) discovers universal constants in the period-doubling route to chaos (Feigenbaum constants 4.669... and 2.502...). These appear in many physical systems.

James Gleick's bestselling book 'Chaos: Making a New Science' (1987) brings the field to a wide audience.
moments.takeaway: Chaos theory becomes a recognised scientific framework with applications across biology, physics, economics.

now.title: Chaos and nonlinear dynamics today
now.body:
Nonlinear dynamics underpins weather prediction (ensemble forecasting), turbulence, epidemic modelling, neural network behaviour, climate, financial markets, cardiac arrhythmias.

Weather forecasting now uses ensembles of dozens of simulations from slightly perturbed initial conditions, giving probability distributions for future weather. The forecast horizon is about 14 days for synoptic-scale features.
now.open_questions: Can we extend weather forecast horizons beyond ~14 days? Are there general theories of complex systems beyond specific equations? Why are certain Feigenbaum constants universal — what does that tell us about how chaos arises? Can we control chaotic systems usefully?

items.reflection: Poincaré had the essential insight in 1890. Lorenz rediscovered it in 1961 with a different generation's technology. The mathematical structure of chaos was sitting in their data, waiting to be noticed. How often does mathematics already contain the answer we need, in some other field, waiting to be re-encountered?

moments.title: Diophantus's Arithmetica
moments.body: Diophantus writes the Arithmetica — 13 books of solved equations using letters for unknowns. It is the first systematic treatment of algebra. Much of the work is lost.
moments.takeaway: Algebra is born in late Alexandria.

moments.title: Bachet's Latin translation
moments.body: Bachet's Latin translation of Diophantus inspires generations of European mathematicians — including Fermat, who writes his famous marginal conjectures in his copy.
moments.takeaway: A 1300-year-old Greek text inspires modern number theory.

moments.title: Hilbert's tenth problem
moments.body: Hilbert asks for an algorithm to decide whether any Diophantine equation has integer solutions.
moments.takeaway: Diophantus's problem becomes a foundational question of the 20th century.

moments.title: Matiyasevich's negative answer
moments.body: Matiyasevich, building on Robinson, Davis, Putnam, proves no such algorithm exists. Diophantine equations are undecidable.
moments.takeaway: Diophantine problems are deeply undecidable.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Modern number theory studies many specific Diophantine equations (Mordell, Faltings, Wiles). Some are solved; others remain open.
now.open_questions: What other Diophantine families are decidable?

items.reflection: Diophantus's problem — 1700 years old — turns out to be undecidable. How often does ancient mathematics foreshadow modern impossibility?

moments.title: Newton's fluxions
moments.body: During the plague years, Newton develops his method of fluxions — derivatives as rates of change. He does not publish for decades.
moments.takeaway: Newton invents calculus and tells almost no one.

moments.title: Leibniz publishes
moments.body: Leibniz publishes his differential calculus, with the dy/dx and integral signs we still use. His notation is far better than Newton's.
moments.takeaway: Leibniz's notation wins; Newton's name doesn't.

moments.title: Priority dispute
moments.body: Newton, as president of the Royal Society, packs a 'neutral' committee that rules in his own favour. The dispute splits English and Continental mathematics for a century.
moments.takeaway: Newton wins the priority war. English mathematics loses the next 100 years.

moments.title: Cauchy makes calculus rigorous
moments.body: Cauchy's 'Cours d'analyse' defines limit, continuity, derivative, integral with new rigour. Weierstrass in 1872 completes the epsilon-delta foundation.
moments.takeaway: Calculus becomes rigorous — 200 years after invention.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Calculus is taught to every science student. Notation is Leibniz's; rigour is Cauchy-Weierstrass. Applications cover physics, engineering, finance, biology.
now.open_questions: Can ML do calculus better than humans? When?

items.reflection: Newton was right about priority but lost the notation war. Is being first more important than being readable?

moments.title: Abel proves quintic insolvability
moments.body: Abel, 22, proves no general formula in radicals can solve quintic equations. He prints a 6-page summary at his own expense; nobody reads it.
moments.takeaway: A 22-year-old solves a 300-year-old problem — and is ignored.

moments.title: Abel in Paris
moments.body: Abel travels to Paris, delivers a major paper to the Academy. Cauchy 'loses' it. Abel returns to Norway in poverty.
moments.takeaway: A landmark paper, lost by the senior referee.

moments.title: Abel dies at 26
moments.body: Abel dies of tuberculosis at 26. Two days later, a letter arrives offering him a Berlin chair. He is buried in a Norwegian graveyard.
moments.takeaway: Abel dies before his work is recognised.

moments.title: Galois extends to all polynomials
moments.body: Galois shows polynomials are solvable in radicals iff their permutation groups are solvable. He invents group theory. He dies in a duel at 20 the next year.
moments.takeaway: Group theory is born, then its inventor dies in a duel.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Group theory is now a cornerstone of mathematics, physics, chemistry, computer science. The Abel Prize (since 2003) honours great mathematicians.
now.open_questions: Can groups of arbitrary order be classified more finely?

items.reflection: Abel and Galois both died young, ignored. Their work shapes 20th-century mathematics. How can early-career mathematicians be heard sooner?

moments.title: Cantor's set theory
moments.body: Cantor shows the rationals are countable but the reals are not. There are different infinities. He proves it by his diagonal argument.
moments.takeaway: Some infinities are bigger than others.

moments.title: Continuum hypothesis
moments.body: Cantor conjectures the continuum hypothesis: there is no set whose cardinality lies strictly between the integers and the reals. Kronecker attacks him relentlessly. Cantor suffers depression and is hospitalised repeatedly.
moments.takeaway: Cantor's bold conjecture and his savage opponent break him.

moments.title: Axiomatic set theory
moments.body: Zermelo-Fraenkel + Choice (ZFC) becomes the standard foundation of modern mathematics.
moments.takeaway: Mathematics gets an axiomatic foundation.

moments.title: Continuum hypothesis independent
moments.body: Cohen proves CH is independent of ZFC — neither provable nor disprovable. Together with Gödel's 1940 work, the continuum hypothesis is settled as undecidable. Cohen wins the Fields Medal.
moments.takeaway: Cantor's question turns out to have no answer in standard mathematics.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Set theorists explore extensions of ZFC, large cardinals, forcing. Practical mathematics rarely cares whether CH is true.
now.open_questions: Is there a 'natural' extension of ZFC that settles CH?

items.reflection: Cantor died in a psychiatric institution, attacked for inventing infinities. Why does conservative mathematics so often resist conceptual revolution?

moments.title: Frege's Begriffsschrift
moments.body: Frege founds modern logic. He tries to derive all mathematics from logic. He spends years writing the Grundgesetze der Arithmetik.
moments.takeaway: Logic gets its first modern formal system.

moments.title: Russell's letter to Frege
moments.body: Russell writes to Frege about a paradox: the set of all sets that don't contain themselves cannot exist. Frege's system is inconsistent. Frege replies graciously: 'Your discovery is of the highest interest and... has caused me much surprise and consternation.'
moments.takeaway: A simple paradox destroys 20 years of foundational work.

moments.title: Principia Mathematica
moments.body: Russell and Whitehead write 'Principia Mathematica' to ground mathematics in logic. It takes 379 pages to prove 1+1=2. The work is technically successful but pedagogically impossible.
moments.takeaway: It takes 379 pages to prove 1+1=2.

moments.title: Gödel's incompleteness
moments.body: Gödel proves any consistent formal system rich enough to encode arithmetic contains true statements it cannot prove. Hilbert's dream of complete foundations dies.
moments.takeaway: Mathematics cannot be entirely formalised.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: ZFC is the working foundation. Proof assistants (Lean, Coq, Isabelle) formalise mathematics. Univalent foundations / homotopy type theory offer alternatives.
now.open_questions: Can all of mathematics be machine-checked?

items.reflection: Russell's paradox killed Frege's life work. Frege replied graciously. How should scientists react when their decades of work are overturned?

moments.title: Shannon's masterpiece
moments.body: Shannon publishes 'A Mathematical Theory of Communication' — almost single-handedly inventing the field. He defines the bit, shows channel capacity has a limit, and proves error-correcting codes can approach it.
moments.takeaway: Information theory is invented in one paper.

moments.title: Shannon's cryptography
moments.body: Shannon publishes 'Communication Theory of Secrecy Systems', founding mathematical cryptography. The one-time pad is proved unconditionally secure.
moments.takeaway: Secret writing becomes mathematical.

moments.title: Reed-Solomon codes
moments.body: Reed-Solomon codes — based on Shannon's principles — become the basis of CD, DVD, QR codes, deep-space communication. Voyager's signals from 24 billion km use Reed-Solomon coding.
moments.takeaway: Shannon's theory enables modern communication and storage.

moments.title: Turbo codes, LDPC
moments.body: Turbo codes (1993) and LDPC (rediscovered, 1996) reach within fractions of a dB of Shannon's limit. Mobile phones approach the theoretical maximum.
moments.takeaway: 50 years later, codes finally approach Shannon's limit.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Information theory underlies all modern communication, storage, ML, and quantum computing. Quantum information theory extends Shannon's framework.
now.open_questions: What is the quantum analog of Shannon entropy in deep cases (e.g. black holes)?

items.reflection: Shannon worked on cryptography during WWII and then invented info theory. How often does war funding create civilian breakthroughs?

moments.title: Student's t
moments.body: Gosset, a brewer at Guinness, develops the t-test under the pseudonym 'Student' (Guinness banned employees from publishing). The test handles small samples.
moments.takeaway: Beer chemistry gives us the t-test.

moments.title: Fisher's 'Statistical Methods'
moments.body: Fisher's book introduces ANOVA, maximum likelihood, design of experiments. He pioneers the p < 0.05 cutoff for 'significance' — a value chosen for convenience, not principle.
moments.takeaway: Modern statistical methods take shape — including p < 0.05.

moments.title: Neyman-Pearson
moments.body: Neyman and Pearson propose hypothesis testing with explicit alternatives, Type I and Type II error. Fisher and Neyman feud bitterly.
moments.takeaway: The framework that still dominates testing today.

moments.title: Replication crisis
moments.body: Misuse of p-values has driven a replication crisis. Many fields are moving to Bayesian methods, pre-registration, effect sizes.
moments.takeaway: Fisher's pragmatic choice has caused widespread misuse.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Statistics is central to all empirical science. Bayesian methods, ML, causal inference are reshaping how we draw conclusions from data.
now.open_questions: Can statistical methods catch up with the volume and complexity of modern data?

items.reflection: Fisher arbitrarily picked p < 0.05. A century later it still drives publication decisions. How do conventions become science?

moments.title: Euler's product formula
moments.body: Euler shows the sum over n of 1/n^s equals the product over primes p of 1/(1-p^-s). Analysis meets number theory.
moments.takeaway: The primes are encoded in an analytic function.

moments.title: Riemann's eight-page paper
moments.body: Riemann extends the zeta function to complex arguments and conjectures that all non-trivial zeros lie on the line Re(s) = 1/2. The Riemann hypothesis.
moments.takeaway: One of the most consequential 8-page papers in mathematics.

moments.title: Hilbert's 8th problem
moments.body: Hilbert lists the Riemann hypothesis among his 23 problems. It is now part of the Clay Millennium Prize Problems (2000), with a $1 million reward.
moments.takeaway: More than 165 years later, RH is still the central question in analytic number theory.

moments.title: Trillions of zeros
moments.body: The first 10^13 zeros all lie on the critical line. Numerical confidence is overwhelming; a proof remains elusive.
moments.takeaway: Computer evidence is huge; mathematical proof is missing.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: The Riemann hypothesis remains the most famous open problem in mathematics. Many results in number theory are conditional on it.
now.open_questions: Is the Riemann hypothesis true? Is the proof short or unimaginably long?

items.reflection: Riemann died at 39 of tuberculosis. His eight-page paper would shape the next century. How much can one short paper achieve?

moments.title: Erdős's wandering life
moments.body: Erdős, fleeing Nazi Hungary, lives out of a suitcase for decades, travelling between collaborators. He publishes ~1,500 papers with ~500 co-authors — the most prolific mathematician in history. He calls God 'the Supreme Fascist' (SF) and dreams of a 'Book' with the perfect proof of each theorem.
moments.takeaway: A homeless mathematician with the largest collaboration network in history.

moments.title: Elementary proof of PNT
moments.body: Erdős and Selberg find an elementary (no complex analysis) proof of the prime number theorem. A priority dispute follows; Selberg wins the Fields Medal.
moments.takeaway: A famously analytic theorem gets an elementary proof.

moments.title: Erdős number
moments.body: The Erdős number — number of co-authorship hops to Erdős — becomes a cultural phenomenon. Few research-active mathematicians have Erdős number > 5.
moments.takeaway: Mathematics is a small world, centred on Erdős.

moments.title: Death
moments.body: Erdős collapses at a conference in Warsaw. He had been giving talks; he had a paper in mind. Friends say he died as he wished — 'doing maths'.
moments.takeaway: Erdős died working.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Mathematics is increasingly collaborative — Erdős's mode. Online tools (Polymath project) extend it. Discrete mathematics, his field, is now central to CS and ML.
now.open_questions: Can mass online collaboration solve major open problems?

items.reflection: Erdős had no home, no spouse, almost no possessions. He died working on the next problem. What does his life say about scientific calling?

moments.title: Babbage's engines
moments.body: Babbage designs the Difference Engine and then the Analytical Engine — a programmable mechanical computer. Neither is built in his lifetime. The British government withdraws funding.
moments.takeaway: The first computer is designed but not built.

moments.title: Lovelace's algorithm
moments.body: Lovelace, translating an Italian paper about the Analytical Engine, adds 'Notes' three times longer than the original. She publishes the first published algorithm intended for a machine — to compute Bernoulli numbers. She speculates the engine could 'act upon other things besides number'.
moments.takeaway: The first programmer foresees general-purpose computation a century early.

moments.title: Turing machine
moments.body: Turing's universal machine formalises what Lovelace had glimpsed. The mathematical theory of computation is born.
moments.takeaway: Lovelace's intuition becomes Turing's mathematics.

moments.title: Difference Engine #2 built
moments.body: Babbage's Difference Engine #2 is built to his original drawings. It works.
moments.takeaway: A 19th-century design works exactly as planned.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Computing dominates modern life. ML is reshaping science. Ada is celebrated annually on Ada Lovelace Day.
now.open_questions: Can quantum computers exceed classical for general-purpose computation?

items.reflection: Lovelace, an aristocratic woman in early Victorian England, anticipated general-purpose computing. How much earlier could computing have arrived?

moments.title: Poincaré's conjecture
moments.body: Poincaré conjectures that any simply connected closed 3-manifold is topologically a 3-sphere. The conjecture stands for nearly a century.
moments.takeaway: A statement that seems obvious but eludes proof for 99 years.

moments.title: Higher-dimensional progress
moments.body: Smale proves the analogous result in dimensions >=5 (1961 Fields Medal). Freedman proves the 4D case (1986 Fields). The 3D case — the original — remains open.
moments.takeaway: Higher dimensions fall first. The original dimension is hardest.

moments.title: Perelman's proof
moments.body: Perelman posts three preprints on arXiv proving the conjecture using Ricci flow techniques developed by Hamilton. He refuses lecture tours, the Fields Medal (2006), and the $1 million Clay prize.
moments.takeaway: A reclusive mathematician solves a 99-year-old problem and refuses the prizes.

moments.title: Perelman in seclusion
moments.body: Perelman lives with his mother in a modest St Petersburg flat. He has not engaged with mathematicians since. He reportedly says: 'I have all I want.'
moments.takeaway: The most famous living mathematician refuses public life.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Ricci flow is now standard in geometric analysis. The Geometrisation conjecture (a generalisation) is also proved. The remaining Millennium Problems are: Riemann, P vs NP, Yang-Mills, Navier-Stokes, Hodge, BSD.
now.open_questions: Will the remaining Millennium Problems be solved this century?

items.reflection: Perelman refused $1 million and a Fields Medal. What does his refusal say about the nature of mathematical recognition?

moments.title: Aryabhata
moments.body: At 23, Aryabhata writes the Aryabhatiya, including a remarkable approximation pi ≈ 3.1416, the sine function (jya), Earth's rotation explaining day-night, and the first table of sines.
moments.takeaway: Trigonometry is born in India in the 5th century.

moments.title: Brahmagupta and zero
moments.body: Brahmagupta gives arithmetic rules for zero and negative numbers. He also solves quadratic equations, including with negative solutions.
moments.takeaway: Zero becomes a number, not just a placeholder.

moments.title: Bhaskara II
moments.body: Bhaskara II's Lilavati and Siddhanta Shiromani anticipate calculus ideas, derivatives of sine, and Rolle's theorem. The Kerala school (14th-16th centuries) develops infinite series for trigonometric functions.
moments.takeaway: Calculus is foreshadowed in medieval India — 500 years before Newton.

moments.title: Al-Khwarizmi transmits
moments.body: al-Khwarizmi's books transmit Indian numerals and arithmetic to the Islamic world, and via translation to Europe. 'Algorithm' and 'algebra' come from his name and book title (al-jabr).
moments.takeaway: Indian numerals travel via Baghdad to Europe.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: The decimal place-value system is universal. Recent scholarship credits the Kerala school for proto-calculus more explicitly.
now.open_questions: How much modern mathematics ultimately traces to India, via Baghdad and beyond?

items.reflection: Calculus was foreshadowed in India 500 years before Newton-Leibniz. Why does the standard history start in 1660?

moments.title: al-Khwarizmi at Baghdad's House of Wisdom
moments.body: al-Khwarizmi writes 'Hisab al-Jabr wal-Muqabala' — the book that gives algebra its name. He also writes the most widely used arithmetic textbook of the era, transmitting Indian numerals.
moments.takeaway: Algebra and the algorithm get their names from one Persian mathematician.

moments.title: Khayyam on cubics
moments.body: Khayyam (better known in the West as a poet) gives geometric solutions to all cubic equations using conic sections. He also reforms the Persian calendar to higher accuracy than the Gregorian.
moments.takeaway: A Persian polymath solves cubics geometrically 500 years before Cardano.

moments.title: Sharaf al-Din al-Tusi
moments.body: al-Tusi develops algebraic and proto-calculus methods for cubic equations, anticipating ideas of derivative.
moments.takeaway: Calculus-like methods appear in medieval Persia.

moments.title: Recognition
moments.body: Islamic mathematics is now recognised as having sustained and extended Greek and Indian mathematics during Europe's lull, and as having developed its own original results.
moments.takeaway: A long-undervalued tradition is being re-evaluated.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Modern mathematics owes much to Baghdad's translation movement. Modern scholarship continues to uncover Islamic mathematical innovation.
now.open_questions: How many Islamic mathematical results were lost when Baghdad fell in 1258?

items.reflection: For five centuries, Persian and Arab mathematicians led the world. Why is this so absent from Western maths curricula?

moments.title: Noether's education and Göttingen
moments.body: Noether earns her PhD in 1907 at Erlangen, but as a woman cannot have a paid academic post. Hilbert invites her to Göttingen; faculty colleagues object. Hilbert: 'I do not see that the sex of the candidate is an argument against her admission as a Privatdozent. After all, we are a university, not a bathing establishment.'
moments.takeaway: One of the greatest mathematicians of the century is barred from a salaried position.

moments.title: Noether's theorem
moments.body: Noether's theorem: every continuous symmetry yields a conservation law. The most consequential theorem in classical and modern physics — discovered by an unpaid lecturer.
moments.takeaway: The deepest theorem in physics comes from an unpaid mathematician.

moments.title: Abstract algebra
moments.body: Noether's papers on ring theory, module theory and algebraic invariants found modern abstract algebra. Her seminars at Göttingen attract students who later define 20th-century algebra.
moments.takeaway: Modern algebra is essentially Noetherian.

moments.title: Nazis expel her
moments.body: Nazi laws expel Jewish faculty. Noether moves to Bryn Mawr in the US. She dies of cancer two years later.
moments.takeaway: Nazi Germany expels its greatest mathematician.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Noetherian rings, Noether's theorem, Noether normalisation are standard mathematical concepts. Noether Day, the Noether Lecture, Noether Prize honour her.
now.open_questions: How much of 20th-century algebra would have been possible without Noether?

items.reflection: Noether could not get a salaried position because she was a woman. The world's greatest abstract algebra was done unpaid. How many other Noethers were lost?

moments.title: Bourbaki founded
moments.who: Weil, Cartan, Dieudonné, Chevalley, Delsarte, de Possel
moments.body: A group of young French mathematicians, frustrated with outdated textbooks, found 'Nicolas Bourbaki' — a collective pseudonym. They aim to rewrite all of mathematics from scratch, with axiomatic rigour.
moments.takeaway: A fictional French mathematician begins rewriting all of mathematics.

moments.title: Éléments de mathématique
moments.body: Bourbaki produces dozens of volumes, transforming presentation across set theory, algebra, topology, integration, Lie groups. Their style becomes the international standard.
moments.takeaway: A multi-decade exposition reshapes mathematical pedagogy worldwide.

moments.title: New Math
moments.body: Bourbaki's structuralism inspires 'New Math' in schools — set theory and abstract structures at age 8. It is widely unsuccessful with children.
moments.takeaway: Abstract structuralism doesn't fit primary school.

moments.title: Continued influence
moments.body: French mathematics retains a Bourbakian flavour — abstract, axiomatic, structural. Modern algebraic geometry (Grothendieck) emerged in this tradition.
moments.takeaway: Bourbaki shapes French maths even now.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Bourbaki's volumes are still updated. Their style coexists with pluralist, less formal approaches.
now.open_questions: Is abstract structuralism still the right way to organise mathematics?

items.reflection: Bourbaki is a fiction that produced real mathematics. How can pseudonymity enable creativity?

moments.title: Kolmogorov's axioms
moments.body: Kolmogorov's 'Grundbegriffe der Wahrscheinlichkeitsrechnung' axiomatises probability theory using measure theory. Probability becomes a rigorous mathematical discipline.
moments.takeaway: Probability finally has axioms.

moments.title: Stochastic processes
moments.body: Markov chains, Brownian motion, Itô calculus formalise stochastic processes. Used in finance (Black-Scholes), physics, biology.
moments.takeaway: Random processes get a mathematical language.

moments.title: Black-Scholes
moments.who: Fischer Black, Myron Scholes, Robert Merton
moments.body: The Black-Scholes formula for options pricing uses Itô calculus. Modern derivatives markets ($10+ trillion notional) are built on it. 1997 Nobel in Economics.
moments.takeaway: Random calculus prices financial derivatives.

moments.title: Probabilistic ML
moments.body: Modern ML — diffusion models, Bayesian neural nets — is fundamentally probabilistic. Generative AI is essentially sampling from learned distributions.
moments.takeaway: Probability is now the backbone of AI.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Probability is taught in every quantitative field. Causal inference (Pearl), formal Bayesian methods, statistical learning all build on Kolmogorov.
now.open_questions: Can probabilistic methods solve out-of-distribution problems in ML?

items.reflection: Probability was studied for 300 years before Kolmogorov gave it axioms. Why was rigorisation so delayed?

moments.title: Fermat's little theorem
moments.body: Fermat states a^p ≡ a (mod p) for prime p. He writes the result in a letter, without proof. Leibniz and Euler later prove it.
moments.takeaway: A modular relation that becomes central to number theory and cryptography.

moments.title: Gauss's Disquisitiones
moments.body: At 24, Gauss publishes 'Disquisitiones Arithmeticae', founding modern number theory. He introduces the congruence symbol (≡), proves quadratic reciprocity (his 'theorema aureum').
moments.takeaway: A 24-year-old's book defines modern number theory.

moments.title: RSA
moments.body: RSA encryption uses Fermat-Euler theorems for public-key cryptography. The hardest problem in the world becomes 'factor a large integer'.
moments.takeaway: Number theory becomes the basis of internet security.

moments.title: Shor's algorithm
moments.body: Shor shows a quantum computer could factor integers exponentially faster than known classical algorithms. Modern cryptography is theoretically broken — but only when quantum hardware catches up.
moments.takeaway: Quantum computing threatens classical cryptography.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Internet security uses RSA, elliptic-curve cryptography. Post-quantum cryptography is being standardised (NIST 2024).
now.open_questions: Can quantum hardware break RSA before post-quantum cryptography is deployed?

items.reflection: Number theory was 'pure' for centuries; it now secures the internet. Why do 'useless' fields become essential?

moments.title: Three classical problems
moments.body: Three problems baffle Greek mathematicians for 2,000 years: trisect an angle, double the cube, square the circle — all using only compass and straightedge.
moments.takeaway: Three impossible problems consume 2,000 years.

moments.title: Wantzel's proofs
moments.body: Wantzel, 23, proves angle trisection and cube doubling are impossible using only compass and straightedge. He dies at 33, exhausted by overwork.
moments.takeaway: Two of the three classical problems are settled — as impossible.

moments.title: Lindemann and pi
moments.body: Lindemann proves pi is transcendental. Squaring the circle is impossible. The last classical problem is closed.
moments.takeaway: pi is transcendental. Circle-squaring is over.

moments.title: Origami
moments.body: Paper folding can do what compass and straightedge cannot — it can trisect angles. The geometric tools change the impossibilities.
moments.takeaway: Different tools, different limits.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Proofs of impossibility are now a major theme: Gödel's incompleteness, halting problem, P vs NP. Some problems are intrinsically impossible.
now.open_questions: Are there more 'natural' problems whose impossibility we have not yet proved?

items.reflection: It took 2,000 years to prove some problems are impossible. How often is the answer to a hard question 'it can't be done'?

moments.title: Riemann integration
moments.body: Riemann formalises integration by partitioning the x-axis. His integral works for many functions but fails for highly oscillatory ones.
moments.takeaway: Riemann's integral is the first rigorous one — but limited.

moments.title: Lebesgue's PhD
moments.body: Lebesgue's thesis introduces 'measure' and a new integral, partitioning the y-axis. It integrates many functions Riemann cannot. The dominated convergence theorem becomes a standard tool.
moments.takeaway: A new integral unlocks modern analysis.

moments.title: Lebesgue's leçons
moments.body: Lebesgue's lectures spread measure theory across analysis. By 1933, Kolmogorov uses it to axiomatise probability.
moments.takeaway: Measure theory becomes the language of modern probability.

moments.title: Banach-Tarski paradox
moments.body: Using the axiom of choice, Banach and Tarski show a ball can be decomposed into pieces and reassembled into two balls of the same volume. The pieces are non-measurable.
moments.takeaway: Some sets defy measure entirely.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Lebesgue integration is standard for analysis, probability, PDE. Real analysis textbooks always teach it. Functional analysis builds on it.
now.open_questions: Are there other reasonable extensions of integration beyond Lebesgue?

items.reflection: Lebesgue's PhD changed the course of analysis. Are there other PhD theses out there that could change a field today?

moments.title: Minimax theorem
moments.body: Von Neumann proves the minimax theorem for zero-sum two-player games. The foundational theorem of game theory.
moments.takeaway: Zero-sum games have optimal strategies.

moments.title: Theory of Games and Economic Behavior
moments.who: John von Neumann, Oskar Morgenstern, Princeton
moments.body: The 600-page book founds game theory and applies it to economics. It launches a half-century of formal economics.
moments.takeaway: Game theory becomes a discipline.

moments.title: Nash equilibrium
moments.body: In a 28-page PhD thesis, Nash proves every finite game has a (possibly mixed) equilibrium. The 1994 Nobel honours him. Nash later suffers schizophrenia and recovers in part.
moments.takeaway: Every game has an equilibrium. The discoverer wins a Nobel after surviving mental illness.

moments.title: Game-theoretic AI
moments.body: AlphaGo, DeepMind's Diplomacy AI, mechanism-design auctions — modern AI extensively uses game theory. Mechanism design (Maskin, Myerson 2007 Nobel) designs games for desired outcomes.
moments.takeaway: Game theory now underlies AI and market design.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Game theory is central to economics, biology (evolutionary game theory), CS (algorithmic mechanism design), AI. Auction design generates billions of dollars in spectrum auctions.
now.open_questions: Can multi-agent AI achieve cooperative equilibria? Can game theory predict geopolitical outcomes?

items.reflection: Nash's 28-page thesis won a Nobel and inspired a Hollywood film. How short can transformative mathematics be?

moments.title: Uhlenbeck's gauge theory
moments.body: Uhlenbeck's work on Yang-Mills equations underlies the geometric analysis used in modern physics. Her bubble compactness theorem and removable singularity result are foundational.
moments.takeaway: Geometric analysis gains its foundation.

moments.title: Park City Mathematics Institute
moments.body: Uhlenbeck co-founds the PCMI to promote women in mathematics. She is influential in policy as well as research.
moments.takeaway: Service work alongside top-tier mathematics.

moments.title: Abel Prize
moments.body: Uhlenbeck becomes the first woman to win the Abel Prize. The citation honours her work on PDEs in geometry and analysis. She is 76.
moments.takeaway: The first woman to win mathematics' top prize.

moments.title: Maryna Viazovska Fields
moments.body: Viazovska wins the Fields Medal (2022) for solving sphere packing in dimensions 8 and 24. The second woman ever to win (Maryam Mirzakhani was first, in 2014).
moments.takeaway: Slowly, women break the Fields/Abel ceiling.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Geometric analysis is a thriving field. Uhlenbeck's results underpin modern work on Calabi-Yau manifolds, Floer homology, string theory.
now.open_questions: How can mathematics continue to broaden participation?

items.reflection: It took until 2019 for a woman to win the Abel Prize, until 2014 for the Fields Medal. What does this say about the structures of mathematical recognition?

moments.title: Gödel's letter to von Neumann
moments.body: Gödel writes to a dying von Neumann asking whether theorem-proving can be made fast — essentially asking whether P = NP. Von Neumann dies; the letter is forgotten until 1989.
moments.takeaway: The P vs NP question is asked in 1956 — and forgotten for decades.

moments.title: Cook-Levin theorem
moments.who: Stephen Cook, Toronto; Leonid Levin, Moscow
moments.body: Cook (and independently Levin) proves SAT is NP-complete: if SAT has a polynomial-time algorithm, so do all NP problems. The Cook-Levin theorem founds complexity theory.
moments.takeaway: NP-completeness is born.

moments.title: Karp's 21 NP-complete problems
moments.body: Karp shows 21 important problems (clique, vertex cover, travelling salesman, etc.) are NP-complete. The implications are vast.
moments.takeaway: Hundreds of practical problems are revealed to be equivalent.

moments.title: Millennium Prize
moments.body: The Clay Institute offers $1 million for resolving P vs NP. It remains the most consequential open problem in computer science.
moments.takeaway: $1 million remains unclaimed.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Most theorists believe P != NP, but no proof. Approximate, probabilistic, and parameterised algorithms address hard problems pragmatically.
now.open_questions: Is P = NP? What proof techniques can resolve it?

items.reflection: Most mathematicians believe P != NP but cannot prove it. How does the field handle a question everyone thinks they know the answer to?

moments.title: Chinese 'Nine Chapters'
moments.body: The Chinese 'Nine Chapters on the Mathematical Art' solves systems of equations using what is essentially Gaussian elimination — 1,500 years before Gauss.
moments.takeaway: Gaussian elimination is invented in China, 1500 years before Gauss.

moments.title: Cramer's rule
moments.body: Cramer formalises the rule using determinants. Determinants are studied for a century before matrices.
moments.takeaway: Determinants come first — matrices later.

moments.title: Cayley's matrices
moments.body: Cayley introduces matrix algebra with addition, multiplication, the inverse. Linear algebra as we know it begins.
moments.takeaway: Matrices become first-class mathematical objects.

moments.title: Heisenberg's matrix mechanics
moments.body: Heisenberg uses matrices to describe atomic spectra — without realising he is using them. Born and Jordan formalise. Quantum mechanics is born from matrix algebra.
moments.takeaway: Cayley's matrices become the language of quantum mechanics.

moments.title: ML and GPUs
moments.body: Modern deep learning is essentially massive matrix multiplication on GPUs. NVIDIA's market cap of ~$3 trillion (2024-25) reflects matrix-multiplying silicon.
moments.takeaway: Linear algebra is the underlying computation of AI.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Linear algebra is taught in every quantitative field. Modern AI is matrix algebra at scale. Tensor analysis extends to higher-dimensional arrays.
now.open_questions: Can quantum linear algebra deliver practical advantage?

items.reflection: China invented Gaussian elimination 1500 years before Gauss. How long can a result remain isolated to one culture?

moments.title: Fermat's marginal note
moments.body:
Fermat writes: 'I have discovered a truly marvellous proof of this proposition, which this margin is too narrow to contain.' He claims x^n + y^n = z^n has no solutions for integer n > 2.

He never publishes. Mathematicians spend 358 years searching.
moments.takeaway: A 358-year search begins with a margin note.

moments.title: Frey's elliptic curve
moments.body: Frey suggests a counterexample to Fermat would give an elliptic curve so peculiar it could not be modular. The Taniyama-Shimura conjecture, if proved, would imply Fermat.
moments.takeaway: Fermat becomes a corollary of a deeper conjecture.

moments.title: Wiles in his attic
moments.body: Wiles works in secret in his Princeton attic for seven years, telling no one. In June 1993 he announces his proof of Taniyama-Shimura (and hence Fermat) at Cambridge. A gap is discovered.
moments.takeaway: A seven-year solitary effort, then a gap.

moments.title: Wiles fixes the gap
moments.body: After 14 frantic months, Wiles and Taylor close the gap. Fermat's Last Theorem is proved. Wiles is knighted (2000) and receives the Abel Prize (2016).
moments.takeaway: Fermat is finally proved — 358 years late.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: The Taniyama-Shimura conjecture has been completely proved (2001). The proof techniques have revolutionised arithmetic geometry.
now.open_questions: What other 'famous' conjectures will be resolved this century?

items.reflection: Wiles worked in secret for 7 years. Modern science emphasises collaboration. Is secrecy ever justified?

moments.title: Königsberg bridges
moments.body: Euler solves the Seven Bridges of Königsberg problem — can you cross each of seven bridges exactly once? — by abstracting it to a graph. He proves it impossible.
moments.takeaway: Graph theory and topology are born from a puzzle.

moments.title: V - E + F = 2
moments.body: Euler discovers that for a convex polyhedron, vertices minus edges plus faces equals 2 — the Euler characteristic. The first topological invariant.
moments.takeaway: Shape has a number associated with it that doesn't change under deformation.

moments.title: Poincaré's analysis situs
moments.body: Poincaré founds modern topology in 'Analysis Situs'. He defines fundamental groups, homology, and (in subsequent papers) the conjecture that bears his name.
moments.takeaway: Topology becomes a discipline.

moments.title: Topological data analysis
moments.body: TDA (persistent homology) is now used in ML for shape analysis of high-dimensional data — neuroscience, biology, materials science.
moments.takeaway: Euler's invariant becomes a data-analysis tool.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Topology is central to mathematics, physics (topological phases of matter), data science. Topological insulators and qubits are active research areas.
now.open_questions: Can topology-based ML algorithms exceed traditional ones?

items.reflection: Euler solved a puzzle by abstraction; the abstraction became a discipline. How often does a puzzle launch a field?

moments.title: Leibniz's binary
moments.body: Leibniz publishes 'Explication de l'Arithmétique Binaire'. He sees binary as theological — 0 = void, 1 = God — and corresponds with Jesuit missionaries in China who tell him of the I Ching's binary hexagrams.
moments.takeaway: Binary is invented as a mystical idea.

moments.title: Boolean algebra
moments.body: Boole develops algebra of logic — AND, OR, NOT. Decades later, this becomes the foundation of digital circuit design.
moments.takeaway: Logical operations get an algebra.

moments.title: Shannon's switching theory
moments.body: At 21, Shannon's master's thesis shows electrical relay circuits implement Boolean algebra. The first link between binary logic and circuits.
moments.takeaway: A 21-year-old's thesis launches digital electronics.

moments.title: ENIAC
moments.body: ENIAC, one of the first electronic computers, uses decimal arithmetic — but binary becomes standard with EDVAC and later. Today every computer is binary at base.
moments.takeaway: Binary becomes the world's default computation.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: All digital computing is binary. Ternary, quantum, neuromorphic alternatives exist but binary dominates.
now.open_questions: Will quantum computing replace binary at any point?

items.reflection: Leibniz saw binary as theology. We now use it for everything. Why are mystical-looking ideas sometimes correct?

moments.title: Hypatia of Alexandria
moments.body: Hypatia, daughter of mathematician Theon, teaches mathematics, astronomy and philosophy in Alexandria. She writes commentaries on Apollonius, Diophantus, and Ptolemy.
moments.takeaway: A major mathematician at the late-classical world's leading intellectual centre.

moments.title: Tensions in Alexandria
moments.body: Alexandria is riven by religious and political conflict. Hypatia stays neutral; she is associated with the pagan-leaning prefect Orestes.
moments.takeaway: Politics encroaches on scholarship.

moments.title: Hypatia murdered
moments.body: A Christian mob, possibly stirred by the bishop Cyril, drags Hypatia from her chariot, strips, and kills her — flaying her with oyster shells. Her death is sometimes taken as marking the end of the classical learning tradition in Alexandria.
moments.takeaway: One of the great early mathematicians is murdered by a mob.

moments.title: Reassessment
moments.body: Hypatia's mathematical work survives mostly through her students. She is honoured in art, fiction (Charles Kingsley's novel), and academic mathematics (named theorems, prizes).
moments.takeaway: Hypatia becomes a symbol of intellectual martyrdom.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: The original works of Apollonius and Diophantus survive partly through commentaries by Hypatia and her father. Her life is studied as a moment of scholarly tragedy.
now.open_questions: How much was lost with Hypatia's death and the decline of Alexandrian scholarship?

items.reflection: Hypatia's murder ended Alexandrian mathematics. How often does political violence destroy intellectual traditions?

moments.title: Archimedes's pi
moments.body: Archimedes bounds pi between 3 10/71 and 3 1/7 using inscribed and circumscribed 96-gons. The method of exhaustion is calculus 1900 years early.
moments.takeaway: Calculus, in essence, 1900 years before Newton.

moments.title: Archimedes killed
moments.body: A Roman soldier kills Archimedes during the sack of Syracuse. He is reportedly working on a geometric figure and asks the soldier not to disturb his circles. The Romans had hoped to capture him alive.
moments.takeaway: One of the greatest mathematicians dies at the hands of an invading army.

moments.title: Increasingly accurate pi
moments.body: François Viète gets 9 decimal places (1593); van Ceulen 35 (1610); Shanks 707 — with 527 correct (1873). The human limit is reached.
moments.takeaway: Human pi calculation tops out at hundreds of digits.

moments.title: 100 trillion digits
moments.body: In 2022, Emma Haruka Iwao at Google calculates pi to 100 trillion digits. Modern records use the Chudnovsky algorithm.
moments.takeaway: Pi to 100 trillion digits — far more than any conceivable physics needs.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Pi calculations now test supercomputers. No physical application needs more than ~40 digits (Planck-scale calculations of the visible universe).
now.open_questions: Is pi 'normal' — does its digit sequence look random?

items.reflection: Archimedes' method of exhaustion is essentially calculus. Why did it take 1900 years to develop further?

moments.title: Galton's correlation
moments.body: Galton (Darwin's half-cousin) introduces correlation while studying inheritance of stature. He coins 'regression' from 'regression toward the mean'. He also founded eugenics — a stain on his legacy.
moments.takeaway: Statistics begins; eugenics begins.

moments.title: Pearson's chi-squared
moments.body: Pearson introduces the chi-squared test, the basis of categorical statistical inference. He founds the statistical journal Biometrika and University College's statistics department.
moments.takeaway: Modern statistics gets its workhorse test.

moments.title: Student's t
moments.body: Gosset, working under the pseudonym 'Student' because Guinness banned employees from publishing, derives the t-distribution for small samples.
moments.takeaway: Brewing chemistry gives us the t-test.

moments.title: Statistics outpaces understanding
moments.body: Statistical methods have been widely misused (p-hacking, HARKing). Pre-registration, Bayesian methods and effect sizes are gaining ground.
moments.takeaway: Statistics has revealed deep problems in its own application.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Statistical methods power genomics, ML, finance, public health. Causal inference and probabilistic graphical models extend classical statistics.
now.open_questions: Can statistics adapt to the era of massive observational data?

items.reflection: Galton and Pearson founded statistics and eugenics. How do we honour their statistics while condemning their ideology?

moments.title: Markov's chains
moments.body: Markov studies dependent random variables — chains where the next state depends only on the current. He applies it to vowel-consonant transitions in Pushkin's 'Eugene Onegin'.
moments.takeaway: Random processes can have memory of one step. Applied to Russian poetry.

moments.title: Metropolis algorithm
moments.body: At Los Alamos, the Metropolis algorithm samples from arbitrary probability distributions using Markov chains. MCMC is born.
moments.takeaway: Markov chains become a universal computational tool.

moments.title: PageRank
moments.body: Page and Brin model the web as a Markov chain. PageRank — the stationary distribution — becomes Google's ranking algorithm. A company founded on Markov chains becomes worth >$2 trillion.
moments.takeaway: Google is, at its core, a Markov chain.

moments.title: Diffusion models
moments.body: Diffusion models (DALL-E, Stable Diffusion, MidJourney) are Markov chains learning to denoise images. State-of-the-art generative AI is stochastic process modelling.
moments.takeaway: Generative AI is largely Markov chains.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Markov chain methods are everywhere in CS, statistics, physics. Hidden Markov models still power speech recognition; Markov decision processes power reinforcement learning.
now.open_questions: What is the next major application class for Markov methods?

items.reflection: Markov applied his chains to Russian poetry; we use them for web search. How predictable is the future use of pure math?

moments.title: Guthrie's conjecture
moments.body: Guthrie, while colouring a map of English counties, conjectures four colours suffice for any planar map. He tells his brother who tells his teacher De Morgan.
moments.takeaway: A simple-looking conjecture, asked by a student colouring a map.

moments.title: Kempe's flawed proof
moments.body: Kempe publishes a proof; everyone believes it. Eleven years later Heawood finds a flaw, but salvages a five-colour theorem.
moments.takeaway: A famous false proof lasts eleven years.

moments.title: Appel-Haken computer proof
moments.body: Appel and Haken prove four colours suffice using a computer to check ~1,500 cases. Mathematicians debate whether a proof that can't be verified by hand is a proof at all.
moments.takeaway: The first major computer-assisted proof divides the community.

moments.title: Formalised in Coq
moments.body: Gonthier formalises the entire proof in the Coq proof assistant. The computer not only checks cases but verifies every logical step. The proof becomes universally accepted.
moments.takeaway: Proof assistants vindicate a 130-year-old controversial theorem.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Proof assistants (Lean, Coq, Isabelle) are increasingly used in mathematics. Major theorems (Kepler conjecture, four colour, odd-order theorem) have been formalised.
now.open_questions: Will most major theorems be machine-checked within decades?

items.reflection: A computer-assisted proof is opaque to humans. What does 'understanding' a proof mean?

moments.title: abc conjecture
moments.body: The abc conjecture: for any e > 0, there are finitely many integer triples (a, b, c) with a + b = c and c > rad(abc)^(1+e). The conjecture implies Fermat (for large n) and many other results.
moments.takeaway: A single conjecture that implies hundreds of others.

moments.title: Mochizuki's claim
moments.body: Mochizuki posts ~500 pages of new mathematics — Inter-universal Teichmüller theory — claiming to prove abc. Almost no one in the world understands it.
moments.takeaway: A proof that's hard to verify, in 500 pages of new framework.

moments.title: Scholze-Stix critique
moments.body: Fields Medalist Scholze and Stix travel to Kyoto and conclude the proof is wrong at a specific point. Mochizuki disagrees. The community is split.
moments.takeaway: A bitter mathematical dispute that resists resolution.

moments.title: Unresolved
moments.body: Mochizuki's proof has been published in a Japanese journal he edits; the wider community remains unconvinced. The abc conjecture is not generally considered proven.
moments.takeaway: A proof's social acceptance depends on community engagement, not just logic.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: The mathematical community is grappling with how to handle very long, very technical, very isolated proofs. Formalisation may help.
now.open_questions: Is Mochizuki's proof right? Can the community ever decide?

items.reflection: Logic alone doesn't validate a proof — the community must accept it. What does this say about the nature of mathematical truth?

moments.title: Navier's equations
moments.body: Navier writes the equations of viscous fluid flow — though his derivation is based on incorrect molecular ideas. The form is right.
moments.takeaway: The right equations from the wrong reasoning.

moments.title: Stokes refines
moments.body: Stokes provides a correct derivation. The Navier-Stokes equations are the basis for nearly all fluid dynamics.
moments.takeaway: The most-used equations in continuum mechanics.

moments.title: Hilbert's 23rd problem
moments.body: Hilbert lists understanding of partial differential equations (specifically existence and smoothness of fluid solutions) among his 23 problems.
moments.takeaway: Hilbert pleads for understanding of PDEs.

moments.title: Millennium Prize
moments.body: The existence and smoothness of solutions to the 3D Navier-Stokes equations is a Clay Millennium Problem ($1 million). 100+ years and counting.
moments.takeaway: The equation that drives every weather forecast — and we don't know if its solutions are smooth.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: CFD (computational fluid dynamics) simulates aircraft, weather, blood flow. We get good numerical answers without theoretical proof.
now.open_questions: Do 3D Navier-Stokes solutions remain smooth? Or do they blow up?

items.reflection: We compute solutions to NS every day. We can't prove they exist. What does that say about engineering and theory?

moments.title: Möbius strip
moments.who: August Möbius, Leipzig; Johann Listing, Göttingen
moments.body: Möbius and Listing independently discover the one-sided surface — a strip with a half-twist. Both publish in the same year.
moments.takeaway: A simple twist creates a surface with one side and one edge.

moments.title: Klein bottle
moments.body: Klein constructs the bottle with no inside or outside. It cannot be embedded in 3D without self-intersection.
moments.takeaway: Higher-dimensional weirdness becomes visualisable.

moments.title: Topology in physics
