moments.body: Non-orientable surfaces, fibre bundles and topological invariants underlie modern physics — quantum Hall effect, topological insulators, gauge theory.
moments.takeaway: Möbius's twist becomes part of fundamental physics.

moments.title: Möbius transformations in CS
moments.body: Möbius transformations (the conformal maps Möbius worked on) appear in computer graphics, geometric deep learning, neural network design.
moments.takeaway: Möbius's ideas pervade modern technology.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Topology is now central to mathematics and theoretical physics. The Möbius strip is the simplest non-orientable surface, but the start of a deep field.
now.open_questions: Can topology fully classify higher-dimensional manifolds?

items.reflection: Möbius's strip is a paper toy. It introduced fundamental new mathematics. How often do toys lead to theory?

moments.title: Gauss's Theorema Egregium
moments.body: Gauss proves the Gaussian curvature of a surface depends only on intrinsic measurements, not on how the surface sits in space. He calls it 'remarkable theorem'.
moments.takeaway: Curvature is intrinsic. You can detect it without leaving the surface.

moments.title: Riemann's habilitation
moments.body: Riemann's lecture, attended by an elderly Gauss, defines manifolds in arbitrary dimensions with a metric. He hints at applications in physics. The lecture is later called the most important in the history of geometry.
moments.takeaway: Geometry generalises to arbitrary dimensions.

moments.title: Einstein uses Riemann
moments.body: Einstein, with help from Marcel Grossmann, uses Riemannian geometry for general relativity. The geometry Riemann hinted at becomes the geometry of spacetime.
moments.takeaway: 60 years after Riemann, his geometry describes the universe.

moments.title: Information geometry
moments.body: Statistical manifolds, equipped with the Fisher information metric, form a Riemannian space. Information geometry now informs ML, particularly natural gradient descent.
moments.takeaway: Statistical estimation lives on a Riemannian manifold.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Differential geometry is central to GR, gauge theory, string theory, robotics, ML. Computer graphics use discrete differential geometry.
now.open_questions: Can geometric deep learning unify ML methods on different domains?

items.reflection: Riemann hinted at physical applications in 1854. Einstein delivered them in 1915. How long must a mathematical idea wait for its physical destiny?

moments.title: Mirzakhani in Tehran
moments.body: Mirzakhani, growing up in post-revolutionary Iran, competes in the International Mathematical Olympiad in 1994 and 1995, winning two gold medals.
moments.takeaway: An Iranian girl wins two IMO golds.

moments.title: Harvard PhD
moments.body: Her PhD thesis on simple geodesics on hyperbolic surfaces is hailed as one of the most beautiful in modern mathematics. She produces three papers each worthy of publication on its own.
moments.takeaway: One of the most acclaimed PhDs of the decade.

moments.title: First woman Fields Medal
moments.body: Mirzakhani becomes the first woman and first Iranian to win the Fields Medal. The citation honours her work on dynamics on moduli spaces of Riemann surfaces.
moments.takeaway: Eighty years after the Fields Medal began, the first woman wins.

moments.title: Death at 40
moments.body: Mirzakhani dies of breast cancer at 40. The Iranian government — including Khamenei — issues unprecedented public tributes. Her image is published in newspapers with her hair uncovered.
moments.takeaway: Iran honours her in a way it does few women.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Maryam Mirzakhani Day is celebrated 12 May (her birthday) as the International Day of Women in Mathematics. Her work shapes ongoing research in dynamics, geometry and probability.
now.open_questions: Will more women receive the Fields Medal in the next 80 years than the last?

items.reflection: Mirzakhani broke a barrier and died at 40. How does individual brilliance change institutional inertia?

moments.title: Hardy-Littlewood collaboration
moments.who: G. H. Hardy, J. E. Littlewood, Cambridge
moments.body: Hardy and Littlewood collaborate from 1911 to 1947 — perhaps the most productive partnership in mathematical history. They wrote nearly 100 joint papers covering analytic number theory.
moments.takeaway: A 36-year collaboration producing 100 papers.

moments.title: Ramanujan in Cambridge
moments.body: Hardy brings the self-taught Ramanujan from Madras to Cambridge. Ramanujan's intuitive results are validated by Hardy's rigorous techniques. Ramanujan dies in 1920 at 32.
moments.takeaway: A rigorous Cambridge mathematician midwives a self-taught Indian genius.

moments.title: A Mathematician's Apology
moments.body: Hardy's elegant memoir defends pure mathematics. Famous lines: 'A mathematician, like a painter or a poet, is a maker of patterns.' He boasts his work has no practical use — number theory cannot be applied to war.
moments.takeaway: A defence of pure mathematics — about to be overtaken by events.

moments.title: Number theory in cryptography
moments.body: Hardy's beloved number theory now secures every credit card transaction on Earth. His prized purity has become foundational to global commerce.
moments.takeaway: Pure mathematics becomes essential applied mathematics.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Hardy-Littlewood circle method, prime distributions, and analytic techniques remain foundational. Hardy's Apology is still in print.
now.open_questions: What other 'pure' mathematics will become essential applied mathematics?

items.reflection: Hardy boasted his work was useless. It now secures the internet. Can mathematics ever be safely 'pure'?

moments.title: Game of Life
moments.body: Conway designs the Game of Life — a 2D cellular automaton with three simple rules. Patterns evolve, replicate, oscillate, and can compute. Martin Gardner's Scientific American column makes it famous.
moments.takeaway: Three simple rules produce universal computation.

moments.title: Universal computation in Life
moments.body: Life is proved Turing-complete. Working logic gates and memory have been built within Life. A Life-pattern computer has been simulated within Life.
moments.takeaway: A toy automaton can compute anything any computer can.

moments.title: Wolfram's New Kind of Science
moments.body: Wolfram's book argues simple computational rules generate the apparent complexity of the universe. The book is divisive.
moments.takeaway: Computation may underlie everything — or not.

moments.title: Conway dies of COVID-19
moments.body: Conway dies in 2020 of complications from COVID-19. He once said the Game of Life was the work he was best known for — and he had mixed feelings about it overshadowing his deeper contributions to group theory and number theory.
moments.takeaway: A great mathematician dies during the pandemic.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Cellular automata are used in modelling traffic, biological development, pattern formation. The Game of Life remains a beloved teaching tool.
now.open_questions: Can cellular automata be used for general-purpose computing?

items.reflection: Conway disliked being remembered for Life. How often do scientists' best-known works not align with what they value?

moments.title: Weierstrass's monster
moments.body: Weierstrass constructs a function that is continuous everywhere but differentiable nowhere. Mathematicians call it 'monstrous'.
moments.takeaway: Pathological functions exist; the establishment is horrified.

moments.title: Julia and Fatou
moments.body: Julia and Fatou study iterations of complex functions and find intricate boundary sets. Their work is forgotten for 50 years.
moments.takeaway: Fractals are studied — without the visualisation power to appreciate them.

moments.title: Mandelbrot coins 'fractal'
moments.body: Mandelbrot at IBM uses early computers to visualise self-similar sets. He coins 'fractal' and applies it to coastlines, cotton prices, river basins. The Mandelbrot set becomes iconic.
moments.takeaway: Computers make fractals visible. They are everywhere.

moments.title: Fractals in nature
moments.body: Fractals model lungs, blood vessels, leaves, coastlines, clouds, financial markets. Fractal dimension becomes a useful descriptor of complex shapes.
moments.takeaway: Nature is fractal at many scales.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Fractal antennas, fractal medical imaging, fractal-based image compression. The mathematical theory of fractal sets is rich and ongoing.
now.open_questions: Are there 'true' fractals or only finite approximations?

items.reflection: Computers made fractal mathematics visible — and useful. How often does visualisation create a field?

moments.title: Wartime control theory
moments.body: Wiener works on anti-aircraft fire control during WWII. He develops the mathematics of feedback systems with noisy inputs — control theory's foundation.
moments.takeaway: WWII shoots down planes — and births control theory.

moments.title: 'Cybernetics'
moments.body: Wiener's book 'Cybernetics, or Control and Communication in the Animal and the Machine' founds the field. Feedback is the unifying principle from thermostats to brains.
moments.takeaway: A new science of feedback — across machines and life.

moments.title: Cybernetics in many forms
moments.body: Cybernetics splits into control engineering, AI, mathematical biology, management science (Beer's Project Cybersyn in Allende's Chile). The general field fades; the applications thrive.
moments.takeaway: Cybernetics dissolves into its applications.

moments.title: Closed-loop everything
moments.body: Closed-loop control underlies autopilots, robotics, insulin pumps, climate control, brain-machine interfaces. Wiener's framework persists in every embedded controller.
moments.takeaway: Feedback is now ubiquitous in technology.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Modern control theory uses Kalman filters, optimal control, model-predictive control. RL is, in a sense, learning-based control.
now.open_questions: Can RL fully replace classical control theory in industrial applications?

items.reflection: Cybernetics promised to unify many sciences and largely failed. Yet its applications dominate technology. What happened?

moments.title: Newcomb's logarithm tables
moments.body: Newcomb notices that early pages of logarithm books are more worn than later ones — first-digit '1' must occur more often than '9'. He publishes a brief note. It is ignored.
moments.takeaway: A worn book hints at a deep statistical law.

moments.title: Benford rediscovers
moments.body: Benford collects 20,000+ data values and finds the same pattern: leading digit d occurs with probability log10(1 + 1/d). It is now called Benford's law.
moments.takeaway: A 60-year-old observation becomes 'Benford's law'.

moments.title: Fraud detection
moments.body: Benford's law is used to detect financial fraud — fabricated numbers usually fail to follow Benford. It is admitted as forensic evidence in some courts.
moments.takeaway: Real numbers follow Benford; faked numbers don't.

moments.title: Theory
moments.body: Benford's law is now derived from scale-invariance arguments. It applies to data spanning multiple orders of magnitude.
moments.takeaway: Benford's law is a fundamental property of scale-free data.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Benford is used in tax fraud detection, election forensics, scientific misconduct investigation, COVID-19 case-count auditing.
now.open_questions: Can other statistical 'fingerprints' rival Benford for fraud detection?

items.reflection: Newcomb's observation was ignored for 60 years. Benford gets the name. How often does priority match popular memory?

moments.title: Kepler's conjecture
moments.body: Kepler conjectures that the densest packing of spheres in 3D is the 'cannonball' face-centred cubic arrangement (~74% dense). The result is intuitively obvious but hard to prove.
moments.takeaway: A conjecture that sounds obvious resists proof for 387 years.

moments.title: Hilbert's 18th problem
moments.body: Hilbert lists sphere packing among his 23 problems.
moments.takeaway: Hilbert flags Kepler's conjecture as outstanding.

moments.title: Hales's proof
moments.body: Hales announces a computer-assisted proof. Referees take five years and conclude the proof is '99% certain'. The journal publishes it with disclaimer.
moments.takeaway: A proof so complex its referees cannot fully verify it.

moments.title: Formal proof
moments.body: Hales leads a project to fully formalise the proof in the HOL Light and Isabelle proof assistants. After 11 years, the proof is machine-verified.
moments.takeaway: A century-spanning conjecture is finally accepted with full rigour.

moments.title: Higher dimensions
moments.body: Viazovska solves sphere packing in 8 and 24 dimensions (using exceptional modular forms). She wins the Fields Medal (2022) for the work.
moments.takeaway: Specific exotic dimensions are solved exactly.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Sphere packing in most dimensions remains open. Sphere packing is used in coding theory, materials science.
now.open_questions: What is the optimal sphere packing density in arbitrary dimension?

items.reflection: Kepler's conjecture took 400 years to prove. Are some 'obvious' conjectures fundamentally hard?

moments.title: Hamilton's bridge insight
moments.body: Walking by the Royal Canal in Dublin, Hamilton has a sudden insight: a 4D number system with three imaginary units i, j, k. He carves i^2 = j^2 = k^2 = ijk = -1 into Brougham Bridge.
moments.takeaway: The first non-commutative algebra is carved into a Dublin bridge.

moments.title: Vector calculus
moments.who: Josiah Willard Gibbs, Yale; Oliver Heaviside, England
moments.body: Gibbs and Heaviside extract the vector calculus from quaternions. Physics goes with vectors; quaternions are sidelined.
moments.takeaway: Hamilton's framework is replaced by simpler vectors for most physics.

moments.title: Quaternions in computer graphics
moments.body: Quaternions are perfect for representing 3D rotations smoothly without singularities. Every modern 3D game engine, robotics simulator, and spacecraft attitude controller uses quaternions.
moments.takeaway: Hamilton's apparent dead end is now everywhere.

moments.title: Geometric algebra revival
moments.body: Clifford / geometric algebra revives Hamilton's approach in a higher-dimensional setting. Applications in physics, robotics, computer vision.
moments.takeaway: Hamilton's vision returns.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Vector calculus dominates undergraduate physics. Quaternions dominate 3D graphics and spacecraft. Clifford algebra ties them together.
now.open_questions: Will geometric algebra unify physical formalism?

items.reflection: Hamilton thought quaternions would supersede vectors. They became niche, then crucial for VR. How do we evaluate which mathematics matters?

moments.title: Dantzig's simplex algorithm
moments.body: Dantzig develops the simplex method for linear programming while working on US Air Force planning problems. Soon used for diet planning, oil refining, military logistics.
moments.takeaway: A wartime algorithm becomes the workhorse of optimisation.

moments.title: Kantorovich's LP
moments.body: Kantorovich invents linear programming independently in the USSR. His work goes unrecognised in the West. He shares the 1975 Nobel in Economics.
moments.takeaway: Independent Soviet discovery.

moments.title: Klee-Minty
moments.body: Klee and Minty show simplex can take exponentially many steps in worst cases. The polynomial-time question is open.
moments.takeaway: Simplex is fast in practice, slow in worst case.

moments.title: Karmarkar's interior-point method
moments.body: Karmarkar's polynomial-time interior-point algorithm for LP becomes a celebrity in mathematics. Interior-point methods extend to many convex optimisation problems.
moments.takeaway: A polynomial-time alternative to simplex.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: LP and its extensions (mixed-integer, convex, conic, SDP) are central to operations research, engineering, finance, ML. Commercial solvers (Gurobi, CPLEX) handle problems with millions of variables.
now.open_questions: Can quantum algorithms accelerate LP further?

items.reflection: LP is one of the most consequential algorithms of the 20th century. Why isn't it as famous as Newton's calculus?

moments.title: Erlangen Programme
moments.body: Klein, at 23, proposes that geometry is the study of properties invariant under a group of transformations. Euclidean, projective, hyperbolic geometries are organised by their symmetry groups.
moments.takeaway: A unified vision of geometry — geometry is group theory.

moments.title: Lie groups in physics
moments.body: Continuous symmetry groups underlie physics (rotations, Lorentz, gauge transformations). Lie's theory becomes essential to fundamental physics.
moments.takeaway: Symmetry runs through physics from special relativity to gauge theory.

moments.title: Noether's theorem
moments.body: Noether shows every continuous symmetry yields a conservation law. Klein's vision deepens into a fundamental principle of physics.
moments.takeaway: Klein's symmetry programme yields conservation laws.

moments.title: Geometric deep learning
moments.body: Modern ML researchers explicitly invoke Klein's Erlangen Programme: convolutional nets handle translation invariance, graph nets handle permutation invariance, etc. Architectures are chosen by symmetry.
moments.takeaway: ML rediscovers Klein.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Group theory and symmetry underlie modern mathematics, physics, chemistry, ML. The Erlangen vision still inspires.
now.open_questions: Can the entire modern ML landscape be organised by symmetries?

items.reflection: Klein had a vision that took a century to fully blossom. How long should we wait for a unifying idea to bear fruit?

moments.title: Haar wavelet
moments.body: Haar's PhD thesis introduces the simplest wavelet — a step function basis for L^2.
moments.takeaway: The first wavelet, in a 1909 PhD thesis.

moments.title: Wavelet theory
moments.who: Jean Morlet, Yves Meyer, Stéphane Mallat
moments.body: Morlet (an oil-company geophysicist) develops continuous wavelets for seismic data. Meyer and Mallat develop the multiresolution theory.
moments.takeaway: Wavelets formalised — by a geophysicist and pure mathematicians.

moments.title: Daubechies wavelets
moments.body: Daubechies constructs compactly supported orthogonal wavelets — the wavelet equivalent of the FFT. Wavelets become practical.
moments.takeaway: Wavelet analysis becomes computationally efficient.

moments.title: JPEG 2000
moments.body: JPEG 2000 uses wavelets for image compression. FBI fingerprint database uses wavelets. MRI imaging uses wavelets. Daubechies wins the Abel Prize (2023).
moments.takeaway: Wavelets compress images, fingerprints, MRI scans.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Wavelets remain central to signal processing, compression, denoising. ML methods (e.g. compressed sensing) build on wavelet ideas.
now.open_questions: Can wavelet-based ML methods beat CNNs in some domains?

items.reflection: Wavelets were invented by a geophysicist, then theorised by pure mathematicians, then commercialised. How often does this pipeline complete?

moments.title: Vibrating strings
moments.body: The vibrating string problem requires functions decomposed into 'normal modes' — what we now call eigenfunctions. Lagrange catalogues the modes.
moments.takeaway: Vibration analysis births eigenvalues.

moments.title: Hilbert and spectra
moments.body: Hilbert develops the spectral theory of integral and differential operators. The 'Hilbert space' becomes the natural setting.
moments.takeaway: Spectra organise infinite-dimensional analysis.

moments.title: Spectra in quantum mechanics
moments.body: Atomic energy levels are eigenvalues of the Hamiltonian. Spectral theory becomes the mathematical heart of quantum mechanics.
moments.takeaway: Quantum measurements yield eigenvalues.

moments.title: PageRank and beyond
moments.body: PageRank is essentially the principal eigenvector of a stochastic matrix. Spectral clustering, graph signal processing, eigenfaces — eigenvalues are everywhere.
moments.takeaway: Eigenvalues organise data, networks and quantum systems alike.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Spectral methods are central to physics, ML, network science. Spectral GNNs, Laplacian eigenmaps, diffusion maps.
now.open_questions: Can spectral methods scale to billion-node networks efficiently?

items.reflection: A concept from vibrating strings became central to quantum mechanics and the web. What makes some mathematical concepts so portable?

moments.title: VC dimension
moments.body: Vapnik and Chervonenkis develop a theory of machine learning generalisation based on the VC dimension. Soviet pure mathematics quietly underpins modern AI.
moments.takeaway: A formal theory of when ML generalises.

moments.title: Support vector machines
moments.who: Vladimir Vapnik et al., AT&T Bell Labs
moments.body: SVMs combine VC theory with kernels to give a state-of-the-art classifier. They dominate ML for a decade.
moments.takeaway: VC theory yields a practical algorithm.

moments.title: AlexNet
moments.body: AlexNet wins ImageNet by a wide margin using a deep convolutional network on GPUs. SVMs are dethroned. Deep learning is born — and largely outruns VC theory.
moments.takeaway: Deep learning works without the guarantees VC theory provides.

moments.title: Generalisation puzzle
moments.body: Deep nets have far more parameters than examples but generalise well. Why? Double descent, neural tangent kernel, mean-field theory — multiple theories vie.
moments.takeaway: Modern ML works better than theory predicts.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Statistical learning theory is a major sub-discipline. New theories try to explain why deep nets work. ML drives much of modern computational research.
now.open_questions: Why do deep nets generalise? What is the right theory?

items.reflection: Vapnik's VC theory remains beautiful and partially obsolete. How does theory cope when practice outruns it?
